source.title: Instruction-tuning Aligns LLMs to the Human Brain
source.authors: Khai Loong Aw; Syrielle Montariol; Badr AlKhamissi; Martin Schrimpf; Antoine Bosselut

record.tranche_reason: The study measures similarity between LLM representations and human brain activity, not convergence between independently trained models as described by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported brain-alignment results concern a human-brain target, not model-to-model convergence, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Behavioral alignment is a correlation between model word perplexity and human reading times, not a representational-similarity result. The study also reports many model-by-dataset values in Appendix G; those are not extracted as claim-version results because the measured target is the human brain.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well LLM activations predict human fMRI responses (brain alignment) and how instruction-tuning, size and benchmark scores relate to it. It never compares representations between models, so no version (V1–V7, all model-to-model or model-to-model-feature claims) is tested. It does not cite either original source. A brain-alignment-versus-scale trend is related to the Platonic argument, but it is a different target (the human brain), so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Add three points. The size and knowledge correlations come mainly from instruction-tuned models. The ablation attributes gains to both the added training data and the instruction-following itself. The authors state the trends hold under RSA and CKA and on Gemma/LLaMA-2, though Table 8 shows mixed directions for some models.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses linear predictivity to compare LLM activations with human fMRI responses and evaluates instruction-tuning; it does not apply a method for measuring model-to-model convergence.
record.method_sensitivity: Brain-alignment improvements vary by neural dataset (+6.9% Pereira 2018, +8.0% Blank 2014, +3.8% Wehbe 2014). The paper also reports that some larger models have minimal or no increases, possibly because vanilla models are near the estimated noise ceiling.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction-tuning raised average LLM-to-brain linear predictivity by 6.2% (+6.9% Pereira, +8.0% Blank, +3.8% Wehbe). Some large vanilla models showed minimal or no gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction-tuning increases LLM-to-human-brain representational alignment on reading fMRI datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Brain alignment correlates with log model size (r=0.95 for instruction-tuned models; r=0.92 for all models). It also correlates with MMLU (r=0.81), BBH world knowledge (r=0.68) and NWP loss (r=-0.54). Correlations were weaker on Blank2014.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM-to-brain alignment increases with model scale and world-knowledge performance, a brain analogue of convergence with scale.

record.code_released: www.github.com/brain-score/language; www.github.com/awwkl/brain language summarization; www.github.com/declare-lab/instruct-eval; www.github.com/tatsu-lab/stanford alpaca
record.problems: Brain-alignment measures compare LLM representations with human fMRI, so they do not directly establish model-to-model convergence. Some larger models show minimal or no instruction-tuning gains; the authors suggest this may relate to proximity to the noise ceiling. The Blank 2014 dataset has only 5 participants, which the authors note may increase noise. Some additional-metric validation results are described as trends, but the corresponding table values are not directly comparable to the main reported scale.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix G gives brain-alignment values by model and neural dataset, including GPT-2-family models; these were not extracted because they measure LLM-to-human-brain alignment rather than any claim version. Appendix J reports additional Gemma and LLaMA-2 values using Linear, RSA, and CKA; these likewise measure brain alignment and are not rows for the claim versions. Behavioral-alignment results are omitted because the measure is correlation between model perplexity and human reading times, not representational convergence.

untested.parts: Model-to-model alignment across scale, architecture, objective or data; only model-to-brain alignment is measured.
No vision models or image-caption pairs.
No mapping or stitching between models. The linear maps used go from model activations to fMRI responses.
No feature or circuit comparisons across models.
Metric dependence is examined only for model-to-brain similarity (Linear/RSA/CKA, Appendix J), not for model-to-model convergence.
No model-to-model alignment levels or their causes.

record.verdict_notes: Relation is set to 'discusses' loosely: the paper concerns LLM–brain representational similarity and does not address model-to-model convergence or cite the originals; 'cites_only' would also be inaccurate. Table 8 (Appendix J) actually shows instruction-tuning lowering Linear for Gemma-2B and RSA for both LLaMA-2 models, despite the authors' claim of consistency. This bears only on brain alignment, not on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Model-to-model representational alignment across scale, architecture, objective, or data.
Cross-modal image-caption alignment and its relation to model capability.
Shared features or subspaces across independently initialized seeds.
Mapping or stitching representations between models, relative representations, or unpaired mappings.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Dependence of model-to-model convergence on similarity metrics, settings, or input distributions.
Whether model-to-model alignment is incomplete, plateaus, or is caused by shared training data or objectives.
